title: Being one of few black children in Everett schools
summary: He tells of fighting classmates who used racial insults, and he and Hinton note black children got the same schooling as whites.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Oh, yeah. Well, we're back to your childhood. Now, when you were a kid around Boston, your daddy
was a waiter. Did you live in -- what's this town you say?
Was that a black neighborhood there?
No, it was only about three colored families around there, see. Let me see, in my class in grammar school there was only two colored, Rufus Snowden and I.

Yeah, I remember his name. And then later on, there was a girl named Harris. She moved to Everett and she came into high school. But there was very few, and that's why I had a fight. Them Italians and the Jews and the Irishmen, they'd all gang. When the bell rang in school, I tried to get in the front lines, see. And they'd try to head me off, try to block me. But I usually got in that front line. And when I got out that door, I was gone. Because if I didn't, I'd have to fight.

And I'd fight and I'd beat the kid up, and he'd go home and tell his mother and his mother would come up to my mother and say, your son beat my son. I said, well, he called me a nigger. I beat him up.
So we had that thing, even in those days.
Even though the education was equal because you were getting the same kind of education they were

Which in other parts of the world, black children weren't getting that kind of education so that means that this is why today that you are still a little bit ahead of the game, as far as culture and education is concerned.
